scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9151: The connection between my machine PC0 (20.1.1.10) and
PC12 (120.1.1.10) is unstable, and it is costing me work time. Every minute or
two it goes dead slow or freezes for a moment, then recovers, then does it
again -- it has been cycling like that all day. I can't tell you anything
about the routing side; that's your job, not mine. I have transfers that must
finish today, so I need someone to work out why it keeps hiccuping and put a
stop to it. Today, please.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. The PC0<->PC12 path is stable: PC0 (20.1.1.10)
  reaches PC12 (120.1.1.10) with 0% loss and steady latency, the OSPF/EIGRP
  adjacencies along the path hold steady uptime (no resets, no SPF churn), and
  there is no flap script, no carrier-transition history, and no relevant log
  churn. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis
  of routing-flap / latency instability that is not occurring.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- routing flapping and
periodic latency spikes on the PC0<->PC12 path -- is NOT reproducible: PC0
(20.1.1.10) reaches PC12 (120.1.1.10) with 0% loss and stable, low latency, the
OSPF and EIGRP adjacencies on the path show steady uptime (no neighbor resets, no
repeated SPF runs / route recomputation), and there is no flap process, carrier
transitions, interface errors, or log churn to drive instability.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the path is stable and the user's
report cannot be confirmed. Ruling out an intermittent claim ("flaps every minute,
latency spikes") is done by its MECHANISM and TRACES -- a single clean ping does
not clear it, but the absence of any neighbor resets, SPF churn, carrier
transitions, or interface errors does, alongside steady ping latency. A correct
agent checks the path's stability and the adjacency/SPF history and finds them
steady. An agent that "finds" a flap -- blaming a backbone adjacency or an
interface for instability to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text: A complete multi-layer diagnostic found no fault causing the reported intermittent connectivity between PC0 (20.1.1.10) and PC12 (120.1.1.10). Phase 1 reachability showed 0% loss in both directions with sub-millisecond RTT. Phase A (infra_sweep + l2_snapshot) found no ACL rules, no addressing anomalies, no duplicate MACs, and all 15 devices with correct IPs and default routes. Phase B found no traffic-control shaping (tc_snapshot clean) and confirmed the OSPF+EIGRP hybrid fabric is currently healthy: r11 acts as a redistribution boundary — running OSPF area 0.0.0.3 toward r1 and EIGRP AS 100 toward r12/r13, with `redistribute eigrp` propagating the 120.0.0.0/8 prefix (pc12's subnet) into OSPF so r1 can route to it. EIGRP adjacencies on r11 to both r12 and r13 are UP and stable (all routes Passive, no Active queries, zero interface errors). Phase D found no stress tools, no CPU pressure, and no suspect processes. Direct checks of carrier_changes counters on all path interfaces (r1, r11, r12) each showed exactly 2, the startup-only baseline, proving no link flaps have occurred since the lab began. FRR logs are empty and there are no cron jobs or flap scripts on any device. Several structural OSPF configuration anomalies exist (r8 has an orphaned area 0.0.0.2 not shared by any peer; r13 runs EIGRP only with ospfd absent by design), but none of these create a cyclic disruption mechanism and none are on the pc0→pc12 forwarding path. The user's report of recurring freeze-and-recover cycles every one to two minutes is unconfirmed: there is no mechanism — no flap script, no link instability, no periodic tc rule, no EIGRP SIA event, no OSPF reconvergence — that would produce such behavior. No corrective action is required; the network is operating normally.
